Title: Miniature OLEDs Driven by Memristive Switching Electrodes for Compact Display Configuration
Text:

Miniature OLEDs Driven by Memristive Switching
Electrodes for Compact Display Conﬁguration
Nahyun Kim, Kiran A. Nirmal, Ho Jin Lee, and Tae Geun Kim*
Memristors have emerged as promising next-generation electronic
components with signiﬁcant potential for applications in nonvolatile memory,
integrated circuits, and neuromorphic computing. Recent advancements in
2D materials have further enhanced memristor performance, oﬀering high
on/oﬀratios, low set/reset voltages, strong data retention, excellent durability,
and fast switching speeds. Despite their versatility, the integration of
memristors into display technologies remains relatively unexplored. This
study investigates memristors incorporating a transition metal dichalcogenide
layer, focusing on their switching mechanisms and potential use as electrodes
in organic light-emitting diode (OLED) devices. By harnessing the resistive
switching phenomenon, the proposed system enables compact, individually
addressable OLED pixels without the need for additional switching
components. This innovative approach broadens the application scope of
memristors in display technology and oﬀers valuable insights into the
development of eﬃcient, compact, and high-performance memristor-based
display systems.
1. Introduction
As the demand for high-resolution displays in emerging ap-
plications such as head-up displays and AR/VR systems con-
tinues to rise, the importance of technologies enabling mini-
and micro-sized pixel implementation has grown signiﬁcantly.

Additionally, integrated optoelectronic com-
ponents that combine display and comput-
ing functionalities are attracting increasing
attention due to the diverse requirements
of stakeholders in the consumer electronics
market.[1–3] Organic light-emitting diodes
(OLEDs) are widely used as light sources
in popular display devices, including TVs,
monitors, and smartphones, owing to their
high brightness, low power consumption,
and ultrathin form factor.[4,5] Moreover,
their simple fabrication process and out-
standing ﬂexibility make OLEDs strong
candidates for next-generation displays,
such as high-resolution and stretchable
systems.[6] OLEDs are typically categorized
as bottom-emission OLEDs (BEOLEDs) or
top-emission OLEDs (TEOLEDs), depend-
ing on the direction of light emission.
The TEOLED architecture, with its near-
100% aperture ratio and excellent stabil-
ity against external stressors such as light
and heat, oﬀers signiﬁcant advantages over
BEOLEDs.[7,8] TEOLEDs are also highly compatible with non-
transparent backplane technologies and support a wide range
of fabrication processes.[9] As a result, extensive research has
focused on various TEOLED components, particularly the top
and bottom electrodes, which are critical to overall device
performance.[10,11] Innovative electrode designs such as capping
layers,[12] wrinkled-structured electrodes,[13] oxide/metal/oxide
(OMO) stacks,[14] and omnidirectional reﬂectors[15] have signif-
icantly improved optoelectronic characteristics, including exter-
nal quantum eﬃciency (EQE) and viewing angle. However, most
of these eﬀorts have concentrated on enhancing optoelectrical
properties such as transmittance, reﬂectance, and conductivity.
To expand the potential applications of TEOLEDs in future
high-density, multifunctional display technologies, it is crucial
to develop electrodes that provide functionalities beyond con-
ventional optoelectronic performance. Speciﬁcally, electrodes
with switching capability, computing potential, and mechani-
cal ﬂexibility are required to meet next-generation demands.
A promising approach involves top-emission organic light-
emitting transistors (TEOLETs), which vertically stack organic
ﬁeld-eﬀect transistors (OFETs) with TEOLEDs. This architecture
has demonstrated signiﬁcant potential for high-resolution, com-
pact, and monolithically integrated optoelectronic systems.[16,17]
TEOLETs achieve compact integration by using the TEOLED’s
bottom electrode as the transistor’s gate electrode, thereby re-
ducing the footprint of thin-ﬁlm transistors (TFTs). However,

challenges persist, including the trade-oﬀbetween carrier mo-
bility and luminescence eﬃciency inherent to the organic ma-
terials used in OLEDs,[18,19] as well as aperture ratio limitations
caused by the source and drain electrodes. In this context, light-
emitting memristors (LEMs), which combine resistive switch-
ing (RS) and light emission in a single mixed-phase active layer,
have gained attention as an alternative route toward high-density
integration.[20,21] These devices typically employ perovskites,
quantum dots, or mixed ionic–electronic conductors, requiring
precise control of ion migration,[22] charge transport,[23,24] and
exciton recombination.[25,26] Despite their promise, LEMs face
critical challenges arising from the strong coupling of struc-
tural and functional properties. These include poor reproducibil-
ity, nonuniform spatial emission, limited operational stability,
and diﬃculties in large-area fabrication. Thus, while concep-
tually appealing, their practical implementation remains hin-
dered by intrinsic material instabilities and complex processing
requirements.
In our previous work, we implemented yttrium-iron-garnet
(YIG)-based RS electrodes in micro-LED arrays and demon-
strated a crosstalk-free, passive-matrix architecture.[27] The RS
electrodes were connected in series with micro-LEDs, enabling
control based on their resistance state. While these electrodes
showed excellent switching performance, including high on/oﬀ
ratios, strong retention, and good endurance, they required a
150°C annealing process and a platinum adhesion layer, limit-
ing their ﬂexibility and scalability for cost-eﬀective applications.
Therefore, a key challenge remains: the development of multi-
functional electrodes that are not only easy to fabricate and ﬂex-
ible but also capable of switching while maintaining their opto-
electronic properties. To overcome these challenges, in this study,
we present a novel molybdenum disulﬁde (MoS2)-based memris-
tive RS (MemRS) reﬂective electrode, speciﬁcally Ag/MoS2/Ag
that simultaneously functions as a switching device, reﬂective
electrode, and synaptic element. The MemRS electrode is fabri-
cated using a radiofrequency (RF) sputtering method without any
annealing step, oﬀering a simple and cost-eﬀective manufactur-
ing process. When employed as a switching device in TEOLEDs,
the MemRS electrode provides distinct high-resistance states
(HRS) and low-resistance states (LRS), eﬀectively controlling cur-
rent ﬂow into the OLEDs. The device demonstrates excellent
switching characteristics, including a high on/oﬀratio (≈104),
low operation voltage (3.7 V), strong data retention (≈105 s), and
endurance (≈104 cycles). Additionally, the high optical reﬂectance
(92.5%–93.8%) of the MemRS electrode enhances optoelectronic
performance by improving light extraction and color purity. Its
high electrical conductivity also contributes to reduced driving
voltage and lower power consumption, thereby extending de-
vice lifetime. Furthermore, the MemRS electrode exhibits reli-
able memristive switching behavior suitable for emulating bio-
logical synaptic functions, expanding its application potential be-
yond conventional display use. We believe this innovative inte-
gration of switching, reﬂective, and synaptic functionalities into
a single device marks a signiﬁcant step forward in the design of
multifunctional electrodes for next-generation high-resolution,
compact, and energy-eﬃcient display technologies.
2. Results and Discussion
The key performance metrics of the memristor, including its
RS characteristics, synaptic plasticity, and optoelectronic perfor-
mance (Figure 1a), are highly dependent on the choice of resistive
materials and the device architecture. Figure 1b shows the struc-
ture of a top-emission OLED that can be independently switched
on or oﬀusing the proposed memristor as an electrode, along
with the corresponding equivalent circuit diagram. In this con-
ﬁguration, the memristor is connected in series with the OLED
and functions as the anode electrode. While the overall structure
resembles that of conventional OLED devices, the integration of
the memristor enables selective control of the OLED’s on/oﬀ
state through its RS behavior. To ensure its eﬀectiveness as an
OLED electrode, the memristor’s performance was stabilized, al-
lowing for precise control of the current ﬂowing into the OLED.
The switching functionality of the memristor arises from the for-
mation and dissolution of conductive ﬁlaments (CFs), which is
a key characteristic of its RS mechanism. This feature was uti-
lized to deﬁne the operational states of the OLED. The operating
principle of this memristor-integrated OLED system is provided
in Figure S1 (Supporting Information). The fabrication process
for the memristor-based OLEDs is described in detail in the Ex-
perimental Section. Memristors were fabricated using a combi-
nation of RF magnetron sputtering and photolithography. Sub-
sequently, organic layers were deposited via thermal evaporation
to complete the OLEDs with integrated memristors.
The proposed OLED demonstrates signiﬁcant potential for in-
tegration into driving circuits. Due to its inherent memory char-
acteristics, the CFs formed within the memristor remain stable
unless deliberately reset. This nonvolatile behavior suggests that
memristor-based electrodes could potentially replace capacitors
in certain applications.[27] While this study primarily focused on
the individual on/oﬀswitching of the OLED device, the unique
RS and memory properties of the memristor electrode indicate
its suitability for active-matrix (AM) display structures. In con-
ventional AM architectures, each driving pixel unit typically com-
prises two thin-ﬁlm transistors (TFTs) and one capacitor (2T-
1C), as illustrated inFigure S2 (Supporting Information). In con-
trast, the proposed memristor-based OLED employs the mem-
ristor as the anode, eliminating the need for a dedicated capac-
itor and simplifying the pixel circuit to a single driving transis-
tor (d-TFT). This innovative conﬁguration not only reduces the
complexity of the driving circuitry but also enables higher inte-
gration density in AM driving systems. The simpliﬁed design of-
fers enhanced potential for developing compact, power-eﬃcient,
and scalable display technologies, highlighting the transforma-
tive role of memristor-based electrodes in the next generation of
display systems.
Figure 2a illustrates the structure of the MoS2-based memris-
tive electrode (MME) in a crossbar array conﬁguration composed
of Ag/MoS2/Ag, along with Transmission electron microscopy
(TEM) and energy dispersive X-ray (EDX) mapping results for
each layer. Both the MoS2 and Ag layers were successfully de-
posited onto a glass substrate using a straightforward RF sputter-
ing process. The MoS2 ﬁlm was deposited using RF magnetron

sputtering with a 99.79% pure MoS2 target. The entire MME was
fabricated without the need for additional complex processing
steps. Figure 2b presents the Raman spectra of the MoS2 thin
ﬁlms, showing characteristic peaks corresponding to the E1
2g and
A1g active vibrational modes at 381.6 and 408.2 cm−1, respectively.
These values are in close agreement with those reported in previ-
ous studies.[28,29] The E1
2g
mode originates from in-plane vibra-
tions of Mo and S atoms, while the A1g mode corresponds to out-
of-plane vibrations of S atoms.[30] Raman spectroscopy serves as
an eﬀective tool for identifying the number of MoS2 layers.[31,32]
Compared to the E1
2g peak and A1g peaks of the single-layer
MoS2 material,[33] the E1
2g peak shifted to a higher frequency,
while the A1g peak shifted to a lower frequency. The observed fre-
quency diﬀerence (D = 26.6) aligned with the predictions for the
multilayer MoS2 structure, conﬁrming that the prepared MoS2
ﬁlms were multilayered. The multilayer structure provides signif-
icantly enhanced electron mobility and higher current-carrying
capacity, which in turn enables eﬃcient charge injection into the
OLED.[34] Additionally, the increased thickness contributes to im-
proved switching reliability and endurance. Multilayer MoS2 also
allows for tunable resistance states and better structural tolerance
during the formation and rupture of CFs, key factors for achiev-
ing stable memristive switching.[35] These advantages collectively
support the suitability of multilayer MoS2 as a robust, scalable
active material for high-eﬃciency, nonvolatile memristor-driven
OLED arrays.
To further investigate the chemical states and composition of
Mo and S in MoS2, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was
performed. Figure 2c,d presents the high-resolution XPS spectra
for the Mo 3d and S 2p regions, respectively. The binding energy
peaks at 232.55 and 229.17 eV correspond to the Mo 3d3/2 and Mo
3d5/2 states of Mo4+ in MoS2, while a peak at 226.68 eV is assigned
to the S 2s core level, consistent with previous reports.[36] Addi-
tional peaks associated with Mo4+ and possible MoxS𝛾species in-
dicate partial oxidation or reduction processes. In the S 2p region,
peaks at 162.23 and 163.33 eV are attributed to the S 2p3/2 and S
2p1/2 states of divalent sulﬁde ions (S2−). The Mo-to-S atomic ratio
was determined to be 1:1.13, revealing the presence of sulfur va-
cancies (SVs). These SVs are known to enhance the switching per-
formance of memristive devices by enabling multilevel resistive
states through interactions with mobile metal ions.[37,38] Accord-
ingly, the RS behavior in our device is most plausibly governed
by the migration of metal ions from the active electrode, assisted
by SV-mediated transport and trapping. Crucially, SVs do not act
merely as passive structural defects; they serve as active sites that
facilitate metal-ion injection, migration, and anchoring, thereby
directly contributing to the formation and rupture of CFs.[39–44]
To validate this mechanism, we examined the interplay between
Ag ion migration and SV dynamics. The RS behavior is attributed
to the reversible formation and disruption of Ag-based CFs, me-
diated by SVs, as schematically illustrated in Figure S3a (Sup-
porting Information). Conductive atomic force microscopy (C-
AFM) further supports this mechanism: well-deﬁned conductive
regions appear in the LRS, whereas negligible current is detected
in the HRS, conﬁrming a ﬁlamentary switching model based
on localized conduction pathways associated with SVs (Figure
S3b, Supporting Information). The role of SVs in the RS process
was further examined by XPS analysis of the S 2p core level be-
fore and after electrical biasing. The as-deposited MoS2 ﬁlms ini-
tially exhibited a Mo:S atomic ratio of ≈1:1.13, indicating intrin-
sic sulfur deﬁciencies. After electroforming and repeated switch-
ing cycles, the S 2p3/2 (≈162.2 eV) and S 2p1/2 (≈163.4 eV) peaks
showed a marked decrease in intensity (Figure S3c, Supporting
Information), consistent with a reduction in sulfur content. This
change likely arises from electric-ﬁeld-induced sulfur migration
or Joule heating, which generates or enhances SVs during device

In the MME, excellent RS performance is typically character-
ized by a low switching voltage, fast operation speed, and long re-
tention times. RS behavior is usually evaluated by applying a bias
to the silver (Ag) electrode. As illustrated in Figure 3a, the metal–
insulator–metal (MIM) structure exhibits both unipolar and bipo-
lar RS behavior, wherein the MoS2 layer transitions between the
LRS and HRS under either positive or negative bias.[45,46] In
this study, the unipolar switching mode was applied to drive the
OLED, as shown in Figure 3b. The electrical properties of the
MME, measured under a constant current (CC) of 1 mA, demon-
strated stable RS characteristics. Additional data showing con-
sistent RS behavior across a range of CC values (0.01 to 1 mA)
are provided inFigure S4a,b (Supporting Information). The mul-
tilevel resistance states of the memristor present a signiﬁcant ad-
vantage for controlling the driving current in AM OLEDs. Apply-
ing diﬀerent CC values during the set process allows for the sta-
ble formation of conductive ﬁlaments, enabling precise current
injection.
The ability to modulate OLED brightness through precise con-
trol of the driving current, enabled by multiple well-deﬁned re-
sistance states (LRS 1 to LRS 3) in the memristor, is crucial for
applications such as analog grayscale control and advanced pixel-
driving schemes in high-resolution display systems. As shown
in Figure S5a (Supporting Information), the memristor exhibits
stable multilevel low-resistance states (LRS 1, LRS 2, and LRS
3) when programmed under increasing compliance currents of
0.01, 0.1, and 1 mA, respectively. These discrete resistance levels
allow accurate and reproducible analog modulation of the driv-
ing current injected into the OLED. At a ﬁxed driving voltage of
8 V, the OLED current (mA), luminance (cd m−2), and power ef-
ﬁciency (lm W−1) were measured for each resistance state. The
results show a monotonic increase in luminance with decreas-
ing resistance, conﬁrming a direct and controllable correlation
between the memristor state and OLED brightness. These ﬁnd-
ings validate the feasibility of analog grayscale modulation using
multilevel memristor states. The power eﬃciency, ranging from

area (800 μm × 800 μm) and demonstrates that brightness con-

EL spectra (Figure S5b, Supporting Information) exhibit a consis-

that brightness modulation is purely current-driven and does not
cause spectral shifts. The gradual increase in EL intensity from
LRS 1 to LRS 3 further supports this conclusion. A corresponding
photoemission image (Figure S5c, Supporting Information) vi-
sually conﬁrms the luminance variation across resistance states,
with no emission observed in the HRS and progressively brighter
emission from LRS 1 to LRS 3. Collectively, these results provide
direct experimental evidence of analog multi-bit control through
memristor-driven current modulation, an essential functionality
for neuromorphic vision systems and next-generation grayscale
display applications.
The I–V curves in Figure 3b exhibit threshold-type volatile RS
behavior. Speciﬁcally, the MME switches abruptly to the LRS at a
threshold voltage of 1.83 V, with the current rising sharply from
≈10 pA to the CC limit—indicating a transition from HRS (OFF)
to LRS (ON). When the voltage is reduced, the device reverts to
the oﬀstate near 0.6 V. This low threshold voltage is attributed to
the enhanced migration of Ag ions, which is facilitated by abun-
dant defect and trap states within the MoS2 layer. These local-
ized states lower the energy barrier for ﬁlament formation, en-
abling RS at reduced operating voltages. As a result, the MME
achieves high selectivity (> 104) and a low oﬀ-current (< 10−7
A), eﬀectively minimizing leakage current in the cross-point ar-
chitecture. The device shows average threshold voltages of 0.57
and 1.9 V, with respective ﬂuctuations (ΔV) of 0.26 and 0.33 V
(Figure 3c). To further evaluate the transient response charac-
teristics essential for display applications, voltage-pulse switch-
ing measurements were performed. The MME exhibited a fast
SET/RESET response, with a rise and fall time of 200 ns (Figure
S6, Supporting Information), meeting the temporal resolution
requirements for displays operating at refresh rates above 60 Hz.
These results conﬁrm the suitability of the MME for video-rate
driving conditions.
Device reliability was further assessed through retention and
endurance tests (Figure 3d,e). The MME demonstrated outstand-
ing endurance over ≈104 switching cycles and data retention
exceeding 105 s, maintaining an on/oﬀratio of ≈104. The cu-
mulative probability distributions of set and reset voltages and
currents (Figure S7a,b, Supporting Information) indicate consis-
tent switching behavior with minimal operational variability. The
HRS and LRS states exhibited excellent uniformity (Figure S7a,
Supporting Information), while the cumulative threshold voltage
plot conﬁrmed the repeatability of both VSET
and VRESET (Figure
S7b, Supporting Information). To mitigate potential risks of ﬁl-
ament hardening or incomplete rupture, which are inherent in
unipolar switching, a compliance-limited SET and pulsed RESET
scheme was employed. This approach ensured stable ON/OFF
operation and eﬀectively suppressed parasitic leakage, even un-
der prolonged cycling stress (Figure S8, Supporting Informa-
tion). In addition to assessing electrical reliability, we investigated
the thermal stability of the MME during switching operations.
Temperature-dependent measurements (25 to 100 °C) revealed
that, although elevated temperatures induced slight variations in

Compared with previously reported MoS2-based RRAM de-
vices (Table S1, Supporting Information), the MME structure
demonstrates signiﬁcantly enhanced performance. These im-
provements are attributed to the optimized Ag/MoS2/Ag archi-
tecture and the high defect density in the MoS2 layer, which facil-
itates the stable and repeatable formation and dissolution of con-
ductive ﬁlaments. Furthermore, the top Ag electrode in the MME
serving as the anode induces a microcavity eﬀect by optimizing
the optical cavity length between the semi-transparent Ag cath-
odes. Reﬂectance spectra (Figure 3f) show that the MME anode
enhances luminance and contributes to a higher EQE. Notably,
the MME also exhibits stable synaptic behavior characteristic of
memristors, with additional details provided in Figures S10 and
S11 (Supporting Information). Collectively, these results conﬁrm
that the MME successfully integrates three critical characteristics
of memristive devices: reliable RS functionality, stable synaptic
plasticity, and enhanced optical performance. These multifunc-
tional properties position the MME as a promising component
for next-generation optoelectronic applications. To validate the
stable operation and performance of the MME in display applica-
tions, an OLED device was fabricated with the MME serving as a
key component. Figure 4a outlines the conventional fabrication
process for memristor-based OLEDs. Figure 4b (left) presents a
schematic diagram of a single-pixel OLED device, alongside a cir-
cuit diagram of three connected pixels used to demonstrate inde-
pendent on/oﬀcontrol. The emission image shown in Figure 4b
(right) conﬁrms the successful on/oﬀswitching of the connected
pixels driven by the MME-based OLED. Notably, each pixel can
be individually controlled using a constant-voltage source, elim-
inating the need for additional peripheral electronics. OLED
operation was evaluated by applying a voltage to the MME to
switch its resistance state, followed by current injection to initi-
ate light emission. A detailed explanation of the emission mecha-
nism and operating principle is provided in Figure S12 (Support-
ing Information). Figure 4c–f displays the energy level diagram
of the OLED and the electrical performance of the connected
pixels.
The single MoS2-based OLEDs exhibited a turn-on voltage of
3.5 V (at 1 cd m−2), and the luminance increased linearly with
applied voltage, reaching ≥1200 cd m−2 at 10 V, conﬁrming sta-
ble electroluminescent behavior. The performance of the OLED
pixel array was further compared with that of single-pixel devices
using both MME and Ag electrodes (Figure S13, Supporting In-
formation). The MME-based single device achieved a maximum
EQE of 12.45%, compared to 11.02% for the Ag-based reference,
corresponding to a relative enhancement of ≈12.9%. In addition,
the MME-based OLED demonstrated higher current eﬃciency
(11.64 cd A−1) and power eﬃciency (10.5 lm W−1) than the Ag-
based device (9.93 cd A−1 and 8.72 lm W−1, respectively) under
identical driving conditions. Similar performance improvements
were consistently observed in pixel-array operation, conﬁrming
the robustness and scalability of the MME structure. The MME-
based array OLED exhibited a maximum current eﬃciency of
10.44 cd A−1 and a power eﬃciency of 7.91 lm W−1, while the Ag-
based reference array showed slightly lower values of 9.56 cd A−1
and 7.80 lm W−1, respectively. These results collectively demon-
strate the enhanced charge injection and light-extraction capabil-
ities of the MME architecture. A summary of the performance
comparison between single-pixel and array devices is provided in
Table S2 (Supporting Information). Table S3 (Supporting Infor-
mation) also shows a comparison of key performance parameters
of the proposed MME with previously reported electrodes (e.g.,
Ag) used in blue top-emitting TADF-OLEDs.
Minor variations in the performance of the OLED pixel ar-
ray compared to single devices were attributed to leakage cur-
rents and diﬀerences in the eﬀective light-emitting area due to
wiring. Notably, gradual increases in the Vdd (4–9 V) during the
set state resulted in distinguishable changes in emission inten-
sity (Figure S14, Supporting Information). At Vdd = 9 V, the max-
imum luminance reached 936.95 cd m−2, suﬃcient for prac-
tical display applications, demonstrating the MME’s capability
to stably drive OLED emission. Importantly, the RS characteris-
tics of the MME enabled self-controlled on/oﬀswitching of the
OLED without requiring additional transistors, ensuring stable
current injections. These features underscore the potential of
MME-driven OLEDs for integration into crossbar matrix struc-
tures, including structured lighting panels and AM displays. To
evaluate the operational stability, we investigated the impact of
RS cycling on OLED emission characteristics (Figure 4g–h). As
summarized in Table S4 (Supporting Information), key optoelec-
tronic parameters, including maximum current eﬃciency, power
eﬃciency, EQE, and luminance, exhibited negligible degrada-
tion with increasing switching cycles. Notably, the maximum lu-
minance and EQE decreased only slightly, by ≈3.1% and 2.2%,
respectively, demonstrating excellent operational stability under
prolonged switching. These variations fall well within the ac-
ceptable range for practical applications. EL spectral measure-
ments further conﬁrmed device stability, showing minimal vari-
ation, with peak emission wavelength shifts of less than 1 nm
and FWHM changes within 2%. This indicates that neither the
emissive layer nor the interfacial regions experienced signiﬁ-
cant structural or electronic degradation during extended cycling.
To further probe device integrity, cross-sectional TEM and AFM
analyses were performed before and after endurance testing. As
shown in Figure S15 (Supporting Information), no apparent in-
terfacial damage or layer interdiﬀusion was observed between
the Ag-based multilayer metal electrode and the organic emis-
sive stack (MoO3/mCP≈). AFM measurements also conﬁrmed
stable surface morphology, with Ra variations remaining within
± 0.02 nm. Moreover, cross-sectional TEM–EDS mapping con-
ducted before and after repeated RS operation revealed no de-
tectable Ag signal within the organic emissive layers, includ-
ing MoO3, mCP, and the emissive region. This strongly sug-
gests that metal ion diﬀusion and interfacial intermixing did
not occur during cycling. These results highlight the critical
role of the MoO3 and mCP interfacial layers in mitigating both
chemical and physical degradation pathways while maintaining
robust charge injection. Consequently, this interface engineer-
ing strategy eﬀectively preserves OLED optoelectronic perfor-
mance during prolonged RS operation. To systematically assess
the mechanical robustness of the proposed device architecture,
comprehensive static and cyclic bending tests were conducted

3. Conclusion
In this study, we investigated the electrical, synaptic, and RS char-
acteristics of a memristor and utilized the fabricated memris-
tor as the anode electrode, referred to as the MME, in an OLED
device. This approach represents a structural innovation for de-
veloping multifunctional OLEDs capable of self-driven on/oﬀ

OLEDs, demonstrating an array conﬁguration in which individ-
ual OLED pixels can be selectively controlled without the need
for additional switching components. This design culminates in
a highly stable and reliable OLED display architecture.
The MME exhibited nonpolar RS characteristics, and the
OLED’s on/oﬀfunctionality was achieved through the MME’s
unipolar switching behavior within the array. This novel inte-
gration of a memristor as the OLED anode presents a promis-
ing strategy for enhancing device reliability while increasing the
integration density of driving circuits. The demonstrated MME
not only enabled independent on/oﬀcontrol at the pixel level
but also showed potential as a replacement for conventional d-
TFTs and capacitors, thereby paving the way for AM driving dis-
plays. This work addresses the longstanding challenge of circuit
complexity in OLED display systems and introduces a simple,
cost-eﬀective, and practical structural solution. The proposed ap-
proach oﬀers a compelling route toward the fabrication of multi-
functional OLEDs, marking a signiﬁcant advancement in driving
circuit design for next-generation display technologies.
4. Experimental Section
Fabrication of MoS2-Based Memristive Electrode (MME):
The memris-
tive electrode was fabricated using a straightforward photolithography pro-
cess. Glass substrates (2.5 × 2.5 cm2) were sequentially cleaned ultrason-
ically for 10 min each in acetone, chloroform, 2-propanol, and deionized
water, followed by nitrogen gas drying. A positive photoresist (AZ GXR-
601) was spin-coated onto the sanitized substrates at 3000 rpm for 30 s to
deﬁne a photolithographic cross-point pattern with a line width of 15 μm.
A 100 nm silver (Ag) layer and a 50 nm MoS2 layer were then deposited
onto the patterned glass substrate using RF magnetron sputtering (KVS-
2000L, Korea Vacuum Tech) at deposition rates of 0.84 and 0.03 nm s−1,
respectively. The base pressure was maintained below 2.0 × 10−6 Torr,
while the working pressure during deposition was set to 5 mTorr for Ag
and 2 mTorr for MoS2, with a 20 sccm argon (Ar) gas ﬂow. The sputter-
ing power was conﬁgured at 100 W for the Ag layer and 20 W for the MoS2
layer. After deposition, the photoresist was removed using acetone, result-
ing in a mesh-structured electrode. The switching layer and top electrode
(TE) were subsequently aligned orthogonally at a 90° angle to form the
ﬁnal cross-point array structure.
OLED Fabrication:
Prior to OLED fabrication, the patterned MME and
Ag-coated glass substrates were cleaned using the same ultrasonic pro-
cedure described previously. Material deposition was carried out via ther-
mal evaporation in a high-vacuum chamber (base pressure: 10−7–10−8
mbar; Daedong High Tech, Republic of Korea). The hole injection layer
(HIL), molybdenum oxide (MoO3) HIL, 1,3–bis(N–carbazolyl) benzene
(mCP) HTL, 10,10–(4,4–sulfonylbis (4,1–phenylene))bis(9,9–dimethyl–
9,10–dihydroacridine) (DMAC–DPS) emission layer, and diphenyl–bis[4–
(pyridin–3–yl)phenyl]silane (DPPS) ETL were evaporated. The electron-
injection layers LiF and Al were deposited at a rate of 0.5 nm s−1. A
20 nm thick Ag layer was thermally evaporated through a cathode shadow
mask at a rate of 1 nm s−1. The OLED emission area was deﬁned as
0.36 mm2 (600 μm × 600 μm) by the overlap between the MME anode and
the Ag cathode. OLED characteristics—including current density–voltage–
luminance (J–V–L) behavior, electroluminescent (EL) intensity, EQE, cur-
rent eﬃciency, and power eﬃciency—were measured using a source meter
(Keithley SMU 2400) and a spectroradiometer (CS-2000, Konica Minolta)
within an OLED I–V–L Test System (M6100, McScience).
Instruments
and
Measurements:
All
electrical
and
optical
measurements—including
current–voltage
(I–V)
characteristics—
were performed using a linear sweep method on a semiconductor
parameter analyzer (Keithley 4200 A). For electrical tests, either positive
or negative voltage was applied to the TE while the bottom electrode was
grounded. The elemental composition of the MoS2 layer was analyzed by
XPS using a PHI 5000 VersaProbe (ULVAC-PHI). Morphological analyses
were conducted using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and
energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). Via-hole structures in the
MME and OLED devices were fabricated using focused ion beam (FIB,
QUAMTA 200 3D). Cross-sectional images of the multilayer structures
were acquired with a focused ion beam–transmission electron micro-
scope (FIB–TEM; Tecnai G2 F30), operated at an accelerating voltage of
300 kV.
